Q: How can I delete all my payment methods in Google Cloud without providing another primary payment method? A:

enter image description hereJust managed to remove the payment method.

First you have to close all of your active subscriptions or services (ie I had some API Keys, 3 projects, etc).

Then the key part is to close what's called the Billing account too.

After that you'll be able to remove easily your credit card from the Payment method section.

Q: Can Subresource Integrity (SRI) be applied to https://www.youtube.com/iframe_api? A:

Is SRI technically feasible or officially supported for iframe_api?

Can't find anything in the docs saying it is supported.

I guess YouTube would have to "version" their API, by providing individual URLs for each version of the script, for this to make sense from their end - then they could give developers the hash matching a specific version.

Anything like trying to "automate" the hash creation, by having your server fetch the script in regular intervals, and then passing the corresponding hash on to the clients, would not make much sense. Even if YouTube delivered the exact same script to every requester worldwide at the same moment (don't know if they do?) - you would only be applying "blind trust" to the script then. If YouTube got hacked, and the attackers were able to serve compromised code via their systems - your server would still just calculate the hash for the manipulated code it receives, and telling clients it was "safe" by passing them that hash.

I've seen some projects download the JS file from YouTube and host it locally - but I couldn't tell you if everything will then work as expected, or if some parts might require that it gets loaded directly from the source. The script appears to mainly serve as loader for a second script, with a "dynamic" looking URL - not sure if YouTube will keep serving that second script under the same URL "forever", even if the reference in their own online version of /iframe_api changes over time.

Last but not least, it appears to be possible to do most stuff the YouTube Iframe API script does, yourself - since it basically comes down to cross-domain communication between the iframe and the parent page via postMessage. So you could implement the necessary things in a script all of your own, that you are then in complete control of - and you therefor can also calculate the hash for yourself. (More on that, if you'd be interested: https://medium.com/@mihauco/youtube-iframe-api-without-youtube-iframe-api-f0ac5fcf7c74)

Q: Python Input Queue Issue A:

For a POSIX environment, where stdin is a terminal, you can do this:

import sys
import termios

termios.tcflush(sys.stdin.fileno(), termios.TCIFLUSH)

Q: Machine Learning model predicts correctly on dataset samples but fails on external inputs – how to handle out-of-distribution data? A:

Yes, this is expected behavior: tree-based models like RandomForest do not extrapolate beyond the training distribution, so when external inputs fall outside the feature ranges or joint distributions seen during training, predictions often collapse to the majority class or become unstable; the correct way to handle this is to explicitly treat it as an out-of-distribution problem by first detecting whether an input lies within the training data manifold (using techniques like isolation forests, Mahalanobis distance, density estimation, or confidence thresholds on predicted probabilities), and only then applying the classifier, while also improving robustness by fitting all preprocessing inside a single sklearn Pipeline, using encoders that handle unknown categories (e.g., OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")), avoiding aggressive outlier clipping that shrinks the learned domain, and expanding training coverage with realistic operating ranges or synthetic augmentation; in real-world machine monitoring, the most reliable pattern is anomaly detection for novel conditions followed by supervised failure classification for in-distribution cases, rather than expecting a single classifier to generalize safely to unseen regimes.

Q: How to work with array of maps in Typescript A:

What you're doing does work but I am unsure it does what you think it does. Lets break this down line by line.

First I think you're mixing mutable and immutable ideas here. What your ending a will look is something along the lines of:

const aIsActually = {
    id: "test",
    types: [
        { test1: 2, test2: 5 },
        { test1: 2, test2: 5 } // both of these point to the same map
    ]
}

map.set mutates and returns the map. So your array in types works off of references. The 0th and 1st index of the array have the same reference, which is to the map object map. This is because map.set not only returns the type Map but it specifically returns this.

This is a 4 year old still unanswered question apparently so hopefully this helps?

Q: How to set different environment variables for each managed host in ansible A:

Please see the ansible documentation for this as it's rather explanatory: https://docs.ansible.com/ansible/latest/user_guide/intro_inventory.html

I am editing my initial answer and try to make it more clear. But please note that I am assuming a few things here:

  1. you are using Linux
  2. you use bash as your shell, Linux offers a variety of shells and the syntax is different
  3. when you say export environment variables I assume you mean copy the variables to the remote host in some form and export them to the shell

Also there's a few things left to do but I have to leave it to you:

  • You need to "load" the env file so the variables are available to the shell (export), you can add an extra line to the ".bashrc" file to source the file, like "source /etc/env_variables", but that will depend on how you want to use the vars. You can easily do that with your shell script or with ansible (lineinfile)

  • I recommend you use a separate file like I did and don't edit the bashrc adding all the variables. It will make you life easier in the future if you want to update the variables.

  • Rename the env file properly so you know what's for and add some backup mechanism - check the documentation https://docs.ansible.com/ansible/latest/collections/ansible/builtin/blockinfile_module.html

Inventory file with the variables:

all:
  hosts:
    <your_host_name1>:
      sys: abc1
      cap: rty2
      jam: yup4
      pak: hyd4
      jum: 563
    <your_host_name2>:
      sys: abc45
      cap: hju
      jam: upy
      pak: upsc
      jum: y78

My very simplistic playbook:

- hosts: all
  become: yes
  become_method: sudo

  tasks:

    -  name: Create env file and add variables
       blockinfile:
         path: /etc/env_variables
         create: yes
         block: |
           export sys={{ sys }}
           export cap={{ cap }}
           export jam={{ jam }}
           export pak={{ pak }}
           export jum={{ jum }}

The final result on the servers I used for testing is the following:

server1:
# BEGIN ANSIBLE MANAGED BLOCK
export sys=abc1
export cap=rty2
export jam=yup4
export pak=hyd4
export jum=563
# END ANSIBLE MANAGED BLOCK

server2:
# BEGIN ANSIBLE MANAGED BLOCK
export sys=abc45
export cap=hju
export jam=upy
export pak=upsc
export jum=y78
# END ANSIBLE MANAGED BLOCK

Hope this is what you are asking for. For windows you may have to find where the user variables are set and adjust the playbook to edit that file, if they are in a text file...
